The Infinite Table

A Dungeons & Dragons round table that never runs out of room. One shared tale, dice that land for everybody, and voice at the table — each player on their own device.

FREE — ALWAYS FREE.

Every seat, every tool on this page — player cards, the shared tabletop, voice, the Dungeon Master’s tools — is free, right here, with no account and no sign-up. The live table needs an internet connection so the devices can find each other through a free public relay. Nothing is stored on any server: the tale lives on the players’ own devices.

Table votes

Any seated person can call a vote, on anything — big or small. The ballot is always the same: Yes / No / Other. A why is optional on ballots and on not-voting — the one exception is a change filed on a closed vote, which requires its reason in a complete sentence. Every vote is a table event: it goes into the Tale, attributed and verbatim, and it is never erased.

One person casts one vote in their own name — unless you have been given the authority by someone else to cast a vote in their name.

That handed authority is the only exception, and it is never assumed: it must be given at this table, by the giver, from their own seat, and recorded — giver, receiver, and scope — before it can be used. A cast made under it still lands in the giver's name, labelled “cast for X by Y, under X's handed authority.” Nobody can cast in another person's name without that recorded authority — that is a hard refusal, enforced by the table itself, not a custom. Voting with a group is a choice, never a requirement: you may always vote on your own, choose not to vote at all, change your own ballot while a vote is open, or make a vote anonymous — and still, nobody ever casts more than one vote under any one name.

Take a seat above to call or cast a vote. Solo counts too — at a solo table you are the only real person voting, and engine NPCs never vote.

Your seat at this table was ended by a vote to kick. Your characters are absent under the Away Rule — out of the living scene, locked, with their state preserved exactly as it was. The vote, its tally, and its whys stay in the record. To sit at this table again this session, the Dungeon Master or host must let you back in below.

Open votes

Call a voteYou write what the vote covers — one topic, or many topics together as one package▾

If you call it anonymous, that is printed on the vote's face before anyone casts: no name is shown with any ballot — not in the tally list, not in the Tale, not in the saved record — while the vote stands. The count still runs by name underneath, so one person still casts only one vote under their name; anonymity hides who chose what, never how many. Whys on an anonymous vote are shown with no name attached.

A vote carrying the no-kick setting can never be turned into a kick: no kick can be switched on under it, whatever its result. It can also be added to a running vote later — protections can be added, never removed. (A vote to kick itself never carries it — it is a kick.)

Locked-vote compulsions — only for a locked vote, set now and printed on its face:

A handed-down vote has no early close: it closes only by reaching its verdict — full turnout, or its timer running out on the tally as it stands (with a full-turnout lock, only when everyone has voted).

The bracket — umbrellas and their sub-votesEvery umbrella vote and everything under it, branching like a tournament bracket — a way of looking, nothing more▾

An umbrella vote stands at the head; its sub-votes branch beneath it, and sub-votes can branch again. Every node shows its state at a glance — open or closed, the live tally or the final result, its timer or its open time, and whether it is waiting its turn in an ordered umbrella. Tap any node to open that vote's own card. The bracket changes no results: it is a way of looking at the votes — every node's record stays exactly as its own vote made it.

No umbrella votes yet — call a vote under another vote and the bracket grows here.

Hand your vote to someone — delegation

You may hand your vote to another seated person — a team leader, a group leader, anyone at the table you choose — for one open vote, or for every vote until you take it back. They then cast in your name: the ballot stands under your name, labelled cast for you by them, under your handed authority, and it counts exactly as your one vote. You never have to vote with the group: handing over is a choice, voting alone is a choice, and not voting is a choice.

Only the giver can give, move, or take back a handover — not the person holding it, not the vote's caller, not the Dungeon Master or host. You may grant, change, move, or retract it at any moment, from your own seat, and every change goes into the record the moment it happens. Retraction is instant for any ballot not yet cast: from that moment, the former holder's cast-for control for you is gone. A ballot already cast while the authority stood stays in the record as cast, labelled with the authority as it stood then — the record never rewrites; a retraction governs the future, not the past. And the owner's hand always wins: if you cast your own ballot on a vote, or change the ballot that stands under your name, that ends the handover for that vote — one vote per name, always.

How voting works at this tableScope, closing, the majority default, kicks, and solo — folded one tap down▾

It works like raising your hand. Nobody calls on you, and nobody gives you the floor. When a question is open, you raise your hand for yes, for no, or for other — whenever you feel it, in your own time. While the question is open you can put your hand up differently. And keeping your hands down is a real answer too — it is recorded as yours, under your name, like any ballot.

The vote is whatever the vote wants to be. The caller writes what it covers: a single topic, or many topics listed together as one package voted as one. Nothing constrains the subject, the size, or the number of topics — there are no categories and no templates.

The ballot is exactly Yes / No / Other. Choosing Other opens a short optional line — “your other, in a few words.” Every ballot also carries an optional why. A why is optional on ballots and on not-voting — the one exception is a change filed on a closed vote, which requires its reason in a complete sentence.

Live and open. The tally updates live for the whole table. Every ballot is attributed — who voted, which choice, their other-words and their why if they gave one — and entered into the Tale verbatim. Votes are table events under the record law: nothing silent, nothing erased.

Closing. A standard vote closes when everyone eligible has voted, or when its caller — or the Dungeon Master / host — closes it early. The result reads plainly: carried, not carried, or tied, with the final tally and whys. Shipped default: a simple majority of the people seated (and eligible to vote) carries it — Yes must be more than half of them. That default lives in the House Rules card, where the Dungeon Master can bend it with real controls there (majority of votes cast, two-thirds, or unanimous) — a change there changes how votes here are decided, and goes into the Tale. One setup stands above all closing: a vote called — or later locked — as everyone must vote cannot be closed by anyone or anything until everyone has voted, as the next paragraph rules.

Everyone must vote — the full-turnout lock. A vote can be set up so that everyone has to vote. While that lock stands, the vote cannot be closed — not early by its caller, not by the Dungeon Master or host, and not by its timer running out. It closes only when every eligible person has cast a ballot or chosen not to vote — every name accounted for. The lock is printed on the vote's face, with the names still outstanding; the close control itself is disabled and says why. If its timer runs out first, the vote simply stays open past the timer, still taking ballots, until the last name is in. The lock can be added to a running vote as a stipulation change — but it can never be removed from one (see Changing a running vote's stipulations below).

Importance. Every vote is called with an importance, chosen by its caller in plain words and printed on its face: light (“it doesn't matter”), ordinary, weighty, or locked (“so important it cannot change”) — and the caller may add their own words beside the level. Importance is what a vote's changeability follows (next paragraph). A game can begin strict and loosen as it goes — a table might start a campaign unanimous and evolve to best-of as the night finds its rhythm — because each vote carries its own importance and its own setup, frozen or flexible exactly as called. And importance only ever moves one way on a running vote: it may be raised, tightening the vote, but never lowered. Lowering a vote's importance to unlock changes to it is the scam door, and it is welded shut.

Changing a running vote's stipulations — importance decides. A vote's stipulations can change after it starts — but how much depends on its importance, every change is a recorded table event (who changed it, what, from what to what, when — announced live, nothing silent, nothing rewritten), and only the vote's caller or the Dungeon Master / host may change one, from their own seat. Light votes — the ones that don't matter — may change freely, even the passing rule. Ordinary votes take the add-only guardrails: a timer may be extended (time can grow, never shrink); the scope wording may be clarified by an appended clarification that rides beside the untouched original; new sub-votes may be added under an umbrella; a full-turnout lock or a no-kick setting may be added (protections can be added, never removed); anonymity may be switched only before the first ballot. On an ordinary vote these are never allowed: lowering or raising the passing bar (the passing rule is frozen at the start — switching rules mid-vote to flip a result either way is the classic scam); shortening a timer below the time people were already promised; removing a full-turnout lock; switching anonymity after the first ballot; changing the question so cast ballots would mean something different; switching kicks on under a no-kick setting; removing or re-parenting a sub-vote that holds ballots. Weighty votes are frozen except adding time or protections. Locked votes take no stipulation changes at all — the record simply stands as called. The honest exit, for every level: if the change you need is not in the allowed set, close the vote as it stands and call a fresh one under the new stipulations — the record keeps both.

Evolving defaults. The table's standing default in House Rules may itself evolve across a session — start unanimous, later best-of, as the game adapts. An evolution step is a recorded event, and it applies only to votes called after it — never retroactively to a vote already open. Every vote is read by the rule as it stood when that vote was called. The future adapts; the present stands.

Locked votes can compel. A vote called locked may carry compulsions, set at call time and printed on its face: it may require full turnout (the lock above); it may mandate kick on or off for its span — kick off means no kick can be called or carried at the table while it stands open, kick on means the person it names is kicked if it carries; and it may require a handed-down result — it cannot be withdrawn or abandoned and has no early close; it must run to its verdict. Some things really are that important, and the table can say so out loud, in advance, on the record.

Each vote sets up its own decision. The table default above is only a fallback. When a vote is called, its caller can set that vote to be decided its own way: a simple majority of the people seated, a majority of the votes actually cast, two-thirds, unanimous — every eligible voter says Yes — or best of, where whichever choice gathers the most votes carries it. The setup a vote was called under is printed on its face before anyone casts, and its result is read by that rule and no other.

The window: a timer, or open time. A vote's caller also sets its window. With a timer — a minute, an hour, whatever is set — the countdown stands on the vote's face, and when it runs out the vote closes itself on the tally exactly as it stands; ballots already cast are untouched. One exception: on a vote under a full-turnout lock, the timer running out does not close it — the vote stays open, still taking ballots, until everyone has voted. With the timer off, the vote stands in open time: no deadline at all — you vote whenever you want while it stands open, and it closes at full turnout or when its caller or the Dungeon Master / host closes it. Either way, the window is stated plainly on the vote's face. And the why rule never moves with the window: while a vote is open, no why is ever required — not for casting, not for changing. The only why that can ever be required is a change filed on a closed vote, in a complete sentence, as ruled below.

Umbrella votes. When a vote is called, its caller may place it under an existing vote. That vote becomes an umbrella: it keeps its own ballot — it is the whole-package question — and the new vote stands beneath it as a sub-vote, a full vote of its own: its own scope, its own setup (its own timer and its own way of being decided), its own ballots, and its own place in the record. The same move works under a sub-vote, so umbrellas nest. A sub-vote's result never rewrites its umbrella's, and an umbrella's never rewrites a sub-vote's — each vote's record is exactly its own.

The bracket. Above, folded one tap down, the votes can be looked at as a bracket — the way a tournament bracket lays out a whole contest: the umbrella at the head, its sub-votes branching under it, every node showing open or closed, the live tally or the final result, and tappable to open that vote's own card. The bracket is a way of looking, and only that: it changes no result and no record.

Order is free, unless an umbrella sets one. Votes do not have to go in any order. Under an umbrella, any sub-vote can be voted on whenever its window is open — first, last, or all at once. An umbrella's setup may set an order, tournament-rounds style: then each sub-vote stays waiting and opens only when the one ahead of it closes. That happens only when it is set that way, and the setting prints on the bracket and on every sub-vote it touches — a waiting vote says so on its face, and its timer, if it has one, starts when it opens.

Vote to kick. A distinct call naming one seated person, on the same ballot — and the person being voted on does not vote on their own kick. If it carries, their seat ends for this session: their characters go absent under the Away Rule — out of the living scene, locked, their state preserved byte-for-byte — and rejoining this session needs the Dungeon Master or host to let them back (the let-back control appears here for the DM/host; a table can bend that in its House Rules too). The kick, its tally, and its whys stay in the record forever.

No-kick votes — and the no-kick setting. There can also be a no-kick vote: a vote not to kick a named person — to keep them at the table. It runs on the same ballot, and the person it names does vote on it. If it carries, that person stands protected for this session: no vote to kick them can be called, and none can be carried, while the protection stands — protection is named on the record with the vote that granted it. If it does not carry, no protection stands and nothing changes. Separately, any ordinary vote may carry a no-kick setting: that vote can never end anyone's seat, and no kick can be switched on under it. Both protections can be added while a vote runs; neither can be removed from one.

One vote per name — and the one exception. One person casts one vote in their own name. The only way anyone casts a ballot under another name is handed authority, given and recorded at this table (see Hand your vote to someone above): giver, receiver, and scope stand in the authority record, and the cast lands in the giver's name — “cast for X by Y, under X's handed authority” — never the caster's. Without that recorded authority, casting in another's name is refused outright. A delegate can never change a ballot they cast for someone else; only the name's owner can.

Handed authority can be given, moved, or taken back at any time. Only the giver, from their own seat. Retraction is instant for any ballot not yet cast. A ballot already cast under authority that stood at cast time stays as cast, labelled with that authority — later changes govern the future, never rewrite the past. If the giver casts their own ballot on a vote, or changes the ballot standing under their name, that vote's handover ends on the spot.

Your ballot is yours to change. While a vote is open, the person whose name a ballot stands under may change it at any time — no permission from the delegate, the caller, or the DM/host. The original cast stays in the record untouched; the change enters as its own entry — “changed by [name] from X to Y” — and the live tally always follows each name's latest standing ballot. After a vote has closed, a change is still heard: it is entered in the record as your new stated position, printed beside the closed vote — but it does not reopen the vote or rewrite its result. One rule is different there: on a closed vote, the why is required — the one place at this table where a why is mandatory. A complete sentence is enough — “I changed my mind.” “I was wrong.” Both count in full, and there is no shame attached to either; “yes”, “no”, or “.” does not, and is refused. Nothing beyond that floor is judged. Everywhere else — every open ballot, every change on an open vote — a why stays optional, always.

Not voting is a real choice. Every eligible person is accounted for by name: they cast, they hand their vote over, they change their ballot — or they choose not to vote on that one, with a why if they want one, and that choice stands in the open list beside the ballots. Choosing not to vote is yours alone: a delegate cannot make it for you, and it ends any handover for that vote. If you later cast while the vote is still open, the cast takes back the not-voting, and both stand in the record.

Anonymous votes. A vote can be called anonymous; it says so on its face before anyone casts. Then no name is shown with any ballot — not here, not in the Tale, not in the saved record — and whys appear with no name attached. Underneath, the count still runs by name, so one vote per name is enforced exactly as on an open vote: anonymity changes what is shown, never how many times anyone can cast.

Solo. Only real people vote. The story engine's NPCs never vote — they are not people at the table. At a solo table your one ballot is the whole turnout, so your vote closes the moment you cast it.

Never played before? Start here — everything explained

You do not need to know anything to play. This section explains every word, every class, and every number on this page in plain language. Read the top layer and you can play. Tap any fold below it to go one layer deeper. Nothing is hidden — it's just folded so it doesn't overwhelm you all at once.

How to use this guide: Layer 1 = the whole game in 30 seconds. Layer 2 = the words. Layer 3 = the classes. Layer 4 = the numbers and stats. Layer 5 = the dice. Layer 6 = a real example of play, line by line. Open only the layer you need.

Layer 1 — The whole game in 30 secondsWhat this is, in one short read▾

This is a pretend adventure you make up together, out loud, like a story where you control one character.

  1. One person is the Dungeon Master (the storyteller). They describe the world: “You are standing at a castle gate. It's raining. A guard is watching you.”
  2. Everyone else plays one character — a hero you invent, like a sneaky Rogue or a kind Cleric who heals people.
  3. You say what your character does: “I try to sneak past the guard” or “I ask the guard for help.” There is no script. You can try almost anything you can imagine.
  4. When the outcome is uncertain, you roll a die. High roll = it probably works. Low roll = it probably goes wrong in an interesting way. The Dungeon Master tells you what happens next.
  5. Then the story continues. That's the whole loop: describe → decide → roll if needed → describe what happened. Repeat for as long as you want to play.

There is no winning or losing like a board game. The point is the story you make together — funny, scary, heroic, or gloriously messy. If everyone had a good time, you played it right.

On this page: the shared story is called The Tale. The little figures on the board are tokens (they show where your character is standing). Normal chat with the other real people — jokes, plans, “brb” — goes in Table Talk, separate from the story.

Layer 2 — The words you'll see everywhereEvery term explained right here, in plain words▾

Character

The pretend person you play. You choose their name, what kind of hero they are (their class), what they look like, and what they do. You are the actor; the character is your role.

Class

Your character's job / type of hero. It answers: “What is this person good at?” A Wizard is good at magic. A Knight is good at fighting up close and protecting friends. See Layer 3 for all ten.

Dungeon Master (DM)

The storyteller and referee for that session. The DM describes places, plays all the side characters, decides what happens after a roll, and keeps the story moving. The DM is not “against” the players — they're running the world so everyone else can adventure in it.

Host

Different job from DM. The Host is just whose open page is holding this online table together. Host starts as DM, but the DM job (the “mantle”) can be handed to anyone else at the table. Host = tech. DM = story.

NPC — Non-Player Character

Any character in the story who is not played by a player at the table. Innkeepers, guards, villains, dragons. The DM plays them (or, in solo mode, this page's story engine plays them from written lines).

Player Character (PC)

The opposite of an NPC: a character played by a real person at the table. When people just say “character” on this page, they usually mean a player character.

Party

Your group of heroes together. “The party enters the cave” just means all your characters together. One person can control several characters — that still counts as part of the party.

Scene

Where and when the story is right now — like a scene in a film. “The Tavern, raining, a stranger at the door” is a scene. The DM sets scenes so everyone imagines the same place.

Token

The small round figure with your avatar on the shared board (the tabletop). Drag it to show where your character is standing. It is just a marker — moving it doesn't change your health or story by itself.

The Tale

The shared story log on this page. Everything that happens in the story lands there: DM descriptions, what characters do, and dice results — so everyone sees the same story.

Table Talk

Chat as yourselves, not as your characters. Planning, questions (“wait, what does d20 mean?”), and jokes go here so they don't clutter the story.

House Rules

Your table's own tweaks. This page never forces a rulebook. If your group wants strict turn order, or wants quest items carried by one person, you write it in House Rules and that's how your table plays.

Quest Item & the Party Pouch

A quest item is a thing the story needs — a key, a map, a magic ring everyone needs to finish the adventure. On this page quest items live in the party pouch (shared, usable by anyone who is present) so the story can never get stuck because the one person carrying the key is offline. Your own sword, cloak, or snacks are personal gear and stay on your card.

Session

One sitting of play — tonight's game, from when you sit down to when you stop. A story can run over many sessions.

Layer 3 — The 10 classes, explained one by oneWhat each class does, who it's for, and what playing it feels like▾

How to choose: Don't look for the “strongest” class — there isn't one. Pick the fantasy you want to live for a few hours. Want to protect friends? Knight or Paladin. Want to sneak and pick locks? Rogue. Want to blast magic? Wizard or Warlock. You can change class on your next character, and your table can rename or bend any of this — the class is a starting costume, not a contract.

⚔ Knight

In one line: The armoured protector in the front line.

In plain words: Wears heavy armour and a shield, fights with a sword up close, and stands between danger and friends. If a monster charges the group, the Knight is the one who steps forward.

Good at: Surviving hits, protecting others, straight-up fighting.

Watch out for: Not sneaky, not magical — solves problems with courage and steel.

Pick this if: you want to feel brave and dependable, and you like simple, clear choices in a fight. Example action: “I raise my shield and stand in the doorway so the others can escape.”

✦ Wizard

In one line: The book-smart spellcaster.

In plain words: Studied magic for years. Can throw fire, open magical locks, read ancient writing, and solve problems nobody else can — but is physically fragile, so friends need to protect them back.

Good at: Powerful, varied magic; knowledge and puzzles.

Watch out for: Low health. Bad idea to stand at the front.

Pick this if: you love clever solutions and big magical moments. Example: “I cast a light spell so we can see inside the cave.”

🗝 Rogue

In one line: The sneaky, quick-fingered scout.

In plain words: Picks locks, spots and disarms traps, sneaks past guards, and strikes from the shadows. The Rogue goes first into the dark corridor — quietly.

Good at: Stealth, locks, traps, sneaky attacks, getting into (and out of) places.

Watch out for: Not built to take lots of hits head-on.

Pick this if: you like secrets, heists, and clever escapes. Example: “I slip behind the guard and lift the key from his belt.”

♪ Bard

In one line: The musician and storyteller who talks their way through anything.

In plain words: Uses music, charm, and words. A Bard can persuade a guard, distract a crowd, inspire friends to do better, and knows a little magic and a little of everything else.

Good at: Talking, persuading, performing, supporting friends, improvising.

Watch out for: Jack-of-all-trades — rarely the very best at one single thing.

Pick this if: you like role-playing conversations and being the face of the group. Example: “I start a song about the captain's bravery — loud enough that we can slip past.”

➶ Ranger

In one line: The wilderness tracker with a bow.

In plain words: At home in forests and wild places. Tracks footprints, hunts, finds paths, and shoots from a distance. If the party is lost outdoors, the Ranger gets them found.

Good at: Archery, tracking, survival, animals and nature outdoors.

Watch out for: Shines most outside cities and dungeons.

Pick this if: you picture yourself with a bow, a cloak, and a good sense of direction. Example: “I follow the footprints — and check if anything followed them back.”

✚ Cleric

In one line: The healer powered by faith.

In plain words: Serves a god or a sacred cause and channels that power to heal wounds, protect friends, and push back undead and darkness. Also sturdy enough to stand near the front.

Good at: Healing (restoring hit points), support magic, turning away undead.

Watch out for: The party will look to you when they're hurt — rewarding, but a responsibility.

Pick this if: you like keeping the group alive and being the moral heart. Example: “I kneel by Wrenna and heal her wounds before she stands.”

🪓 Barbarian

In one line: The mighty, tough fighter who hits hardest.

In plain words: Strength and endurance over armour and tactics. In a rage, a Barbarian hits harder and shrugs off damage. Usually has the most hit points in the party.

Good at: Raw strength, taking damage, smashing obstacles.

Watch out for: Subtlety and spellcasting are not the toolkit.

Pick this if: you want big, satisfying, uncomplicated action. Example: “I lift the portcullis. Slowly. While growling.”

🌿 Druid

In one line: The nature guardian who can become an animal.

In plain words: Draws magic from the natural world — healing herbs, entangling vines, weather and beasts. In fuller D&D rules Druids can shapeshift into animals; at this table, your DM decides how you play that.

Good at: Nature magic, healing, animals, wild places.

Watch out for: Civilisation and metal-heavy dungeons feel foreign to them.

Pick this if: you love animals, forests, and wild magic. Example: “I ask the birds what they saw over the castle this morning.”

◉ Warlock

In one line: The spellcaster who made a deal for their power.

In plain words: Magic didn't come from study — it came from a pact with a mysterious, powerful being. Who is it? What did you promise? That mystery is built into the character and makes great stories.

Good at: Blasting magic, strange and eerie powers, secrets.

Watch out for: Fewer spells at a time — each one has to count.

Pick this if: you want a built-in mystery and a slightly dangerous edge. Example: “I whisper to my patron and fire a bolt of crackling energy.”

☀ Paladin

In one line: The holy knight sworn to an oath.

In plain words: Half Knight, half Cleric. Fights in armour like a Knight, heals and protects like a Cleric, and lives by a sworn oath — protect the innocent, keep your word, stand against evil. Breaking the oath is a big story moment.

Good at: Fighting, healing a little, protecting and inspiring the group.

Watch out for: The oath can put you in hard moral choices — that's the fun of it.

Pick this if: you want to be the shining, principled hero. Example: “I gave my word she would be safe. I step between her and the blade.”

Still can't decide? Pick Knight for simple and sturdy, Bard if you like talking, Cleric if you like helping, or Rogue if you like sneaking. There is no wrong first choice — your first character teaches you what you want your second one to be.

Layer 4 — The numbers & stats, explainedLevel, hit points, and the six classic abilities — what each number actually means▾

This page keeps your card deliberately simple — just three numbers. Here is each one, then the fuller set of stats people talk about in D&D, so the words never leave you behind.

The three numbers on your card here

Level (1–20)

What it is: How experienced and powerful your character is overall. Level 1 = brand new hero, just starting out. Level 5 = seasoned. Level 10 = famous and formidable. Level 20 = legendary, near the top of what's possible.

What it does: As you play and succeed over sessions, the DM may say “you level up.” Higher level generally means more health, better chances, and stronger abilities. Start at Level 1 if you're new — everyone at the table usually starts together.

Hit Points — HP (now / max)

What it is: Your character's health, as a number. “Max” is your full health when unhurt (e.g. 10). “Now” is what you have left right now.

How it moves: Get hurt → HP goes down. Get healed or rest → HP goes up (never above max). Example: You have 10/10. A trap does 3 damage → you are 7/10. A Cleric heals you for 4 → back to 10/10 (you can't go over your max).

At 0 HP: Your character is down and in danger — in classic rules, unconscious and needing help fast. The DM narrates exactly what it means at your table. HP is not your worth or skill — a Wizard with 6 HP can be more powerful than a Barbarian with 16; they just can't take as many hits.

The six classic abilities — the “stats” people mention

Full D&D gives every character six ability scores. This page does not make you fill them in — your table can play without them, keep them on paper, or note them in your title. But other players will say these words, so here is each one in plain language. Each ability answers one question, and when you try something related, that's the ability the DM thinks about for your roll.

Strength (STR)

Question: How physically powerful are you? Lifting, pushing, smashing, swinging a sword. High STR: Barbarians, Knights. Try: “I push the boulder aside.”

Dexterity (DEX)

Question: How quick, nimble, and steady-handed are you? Sneaking, dodging, balancing, picking a lock, shooting a bow. High DEX: Rogues, Rangers. Try: “I tiptoe across the creaky floor.”

Constitution (CON)

Question: How tough and healthy are you? Enduring pain, poison, cold, and long marches. CON also helps decide your hit points — tough body, more health. Try: “I keep marching through the storm.”

Intelligence (INT)

Question: How much have you learned, and how well do you reason? Remembering lore, solving puzzles, reading ancient runes, investigating clues. High INT: Wizards. Try: “Have I read about this symbol before?”

Wisdom (WIS)

Question: How aware and perceptive are you? Noticing things, reading people, gut feeling, common sense. Different from INT: INT is book-knowledge, WIS is noticing the guard is lying. High WIS: Clerics, Druids. Try: “Do I notice anything odd about this room?”

Charisma (CHA)

Question: How strong is your presence with people? Persuading, performing, bluffing, leading, intimidating. Not just looks — it's force of personality. High CHA: Bards, Paladins, Warlocks. Try: “I convince the guard we're expected inside.”

What the numbers usually mean (if your table uses them): 10 is average for an ordinary person. 8 is a bit below average, 12–13 noticeably good, 16–17 excellent, 18+ exceptional. A character is supposed to be weak somewhere — a mighty Barbarian who can't read, or a brilliant Wizard who can't lift a chair, is more fun and more human than a character who's great at everything.

“Modifier” — if you hear it: In full rules each score gives a small bonus or penalty (like +2 or −1) that gets added to dice rolls. On this page you don't need to calculate any of that unless your table wants to — the DM can just judge the roll as rolled.

Layer 5 — The dice, explainedWhat d20, d6 and the rest mean, and what a good or bad roll is▾

The code is simple: “d” + a number = a die with that many sides. d6 is the ordinary six-sided die from board games. d20 is a twenty-sided die — the star of D&D. When this page says “roll a d20,” tap the d20 button in the dice tray under The Tale. The result appears in The Tale for the whole table at once — nobody has to trust anybody's maths or eyesight.

d44 sides
Smallest. Tiny damage, small effects.
d66 sides
The classic die. Common damage & random tables.
d88 sides
Medium weapons & healing.
d1010 sides
Bigger weapons; also used in pairs for %.
d1212 sides
The Barbarian's big axe die.
d2020 sides
The main die. Trying something risky? Usually d20.
d100100 sides
Percentile — roll 1–100 for rare tables & wild chances.

So what is a “good” roll? On a d20: higher is better. Rough guide your DM may use — 15–20 strong success, 10–14 often just enough, 5–9 shaky, 2–4 usually a miss. Your DM sets how hard each attempt is; there is no single pass mark for everything. Trying to jump a puddle is easy; jumping a chasm is not — same die, different bar.

Natural 20: rolling a 20 on the d20 itself (before any bonuses) — the best possible luck. This page calls it out as ★ NATURAL 20 ★ and it usually means a spectacular success. Natural 1: rolling a 1 — the worst luck, usually a fumble: the attempt goes wrong in a memorable way. Both are story gold, not just maths.

When do you roll at all? Only when the outcome is genuinely uncertain and failure would be interesting. You don't roll to walk across a room or talk to a friend. You roll to pick a lock while guards approach, leap the river, or convince a suspicious captain. If the DM doesn't ask for a roll, just say what you do — and it happens.

Damage and healing rolls: Fighting and healing often use the smaller dice (d4–d12). The DM will say which — “roll a d8 for damage” — you tap that die, and the number comes off an enemy's HP or back onto a friend's.

Layer 6 — Watch a minute of playA real example, line by line, so you can copy the shape of it▾

DM (narration): “You reach the Castle Gate. Torches, iron, and a guard who has already decided you look suspicious. What do you do?”

Ana, playing Sella the Rogue (action): “I hang back in the shadows and watch the guard. Does he ever look away?”

DM: “Roll a d20 to see how well you hide and watch.”

Ana taps d20 → 17. DM: “Easily. Every few minutes he turns to warm his hands at the brazier — that's your window.”

Ben, playing Bram the Knight (action): “Then I'll walk up openly and start complaining about the rain, loudly, to keep his attention on me.”

DM: “He loves complaining about the rain. Sella — you're through the side door while he's mid-rant. Inside, you hear something scratching behind a locked door…”

Notice the shape: nobody “took a turn” by force — Ana spoke, then Ben built on it. Nobody needed to know any rules beyond say what you try, roll when the DM asks. The DM never said “wrong answer” — even a failed roll would just have changed the story (“the guard spots movement — ‘Oi! Who's there?’”), not ended it.

Your first five minutes, as a checklist:

  1. Fill in a name and pick a class below (use Layer 3 if you're stuck — or pick Bard, you can talk your way out of almost anything).
  2. Leave Level at 1 and Hit Points at 10/10 if you're unsure. Those are safe starting numbers.
  3. Create a table, join one with a code, or tap Play solo to practise alone with the page's NPCs first — solo is a great, no-pressure rehearsal.
  4. When the DM describes a scene, type one thing your character does in “Your character acts.” Short is fine. “I look under the table” is a complete, legal move.
  5. Roll only when asked (or when you want luck involved), ask questions in Table Talk whenever you're lost, and remember: asking “what can I do here?” is always allowed.

Take your seat

Make your character, then create a table or join one with a table code. Your card is saved on this device only so rejoining is one tap — use Forget to clear it. New here? Every field below explains itself, and the guide above (“Never played before?”) explains every class and number in full.

Hit points (HP) in one breath: hurt → “now” goes down; healed or rested → it goes back up, never above “max.” At 0 you're down and need help. See Layer 4 above for a worked example and all six classic stats (Strength, Dexterity, and the rest) explained.

Claimed Names — the registry

The standing rule for everyone: once a name is claimed on any table, it is claimed on all tables. The registry below is the face — the full law is one tap down. Claimed — locked means only its owner, with their code, can sit under it.

Claim your name ↓Check a string ↓Who's at the table ↑
The standing rule & the unrestricted-names lawOnce claimed, claimed on all tables — and a name can be anything you can type▾

Once a name is claimed on any table, it is claimed on all tables.

That is the rule, for everyone — not a privilege for one seat. A claim made at one table is not a local note. It enters the one shared registry, and every table run from these pages enforces it.

Your name can be anything you can type.

The law protects names — it does not police them. A name itself is unrestricted: any language, any script, emoji, symbols, spaces, punctuation, mixed scripts, long or short — anything a text input can hold. Your name is stored and displayed exactly as you wrote it, every decoration intact. Nothing about its shape — how wild, how decorated, how unusual — is ever a reason to refuse it.

Your name at the table is yours. Anyone may claim one name — in any language, any script, any form of symbols — and from then on no one else can sit down under it, at any table run from these pages. This is not a privilege for one person: the same law covers every seat. The first name ever claimed stands as entry #1:

The registry is loading…

Check a string against the registryMATCH, FOLDS-ONLY, or NO MATCH — checked against the registry’s exact record▾

Paste any string — a name you were sent, a name from a screenshot, your own — and check it against the registry’s exact record. Three answers are possible: MATCH (byte-exactly the recorded string), FOLDS-ONLY (it folds onto a claim but is not the string — an imitation), or NO MATCH.

How a claim made here reaches every tableRecorded in the Tale and the registry’s history; shipped to every table with each new version▾

There is no server holding a live master list, so a claim travels the honest way these pages travel — in the open, on the record, version by version. Here is exactly how it works, with nothing smoothed over:

  • You can claim right at any table. Use the claim form on this page — “Claim your name on this device” below — wherever you are sitting. You do not need to go to a special office or a different page to claim.
  • The claim is recorded twice, at once. It goes into that table’s Tale record — the shared story log everyone at the table witnesses — and into the registry’s append-only history, with its date. Append-only means the entry is added, never edited away: the history itself is the proof of when the claim was made.
  • Claims travel to all tables as registry updates. When a new version of these pages is published, the updated registry ships baked into that version. From that version on, every table run from those pages enforces the name everywhere — the host’s copy checks every name as people join and refuses a claimed name to anyone who cannot open it with its code.
  • If the same name is claimed at two tables before an update ships, the first recorded claim wins. Two tables can, in the gap before an update, each record a claim to the same name without yet knowing of the other. The registry history settles it: the earliest dated claim stands, and the later claim must choose another name. First come, first claimed — decided by the record, not by who argues loudest.
  • Until an update lands, the room still protects you. Inside any one table, the first claim of a name is final for that run — the room-level rule. So a claim protects the table where it was made from the moment it is made, and protects every table from the next published version forward. That gap is the honest seam of a system with no server, and it is printed here rather than hidden.
Unrestricted names — folding is only a key, never a filterAnything you can type is welcome; folding never alters, trims, or filters a name▾
  • A name itself is unrestricted. Any language, any script, emoji, symbols, spaces, punctuation, mixed scripts in one name, long or short — anything a text input can hold is a welcome name. There is no “proper name” test, no allowed-character list, and no tidiness rule.
  • Displayed exactly as written. The name is stored and shown exactly as its owner wrote it, every decoration intact — capitals, spaces, punctuation, emoji, raised marks, all of it. The page never cleans a name up, trims its decoration, or rewrites it into a plainer form for display.
  • Folding is ONLY a comparison key. To check a claim, the page quietly folds a name down to a key — it never alters, trims, or rejects a name for its shape. Folding exists for one job only: catching a copy that is trying to look different underneath while being the same name. The folded key is not your name; your name is what you typed.
  • The gate refuses for exactly two reasons — and no other. (1) The name folds onto somebody else’s live claim and the person sitting down cannot open it with that claim’s code; or (2) the name folds onto a retired name — one that was claimed before and can never be worn again. Every other name, however wild, is welcome.
How a claim protects the name itself — not one spelling of itLookalike letters, decorated digits, and every written form fold into the one name▾
  • A claim protects the name, not a keyboard trick. Before any name is checked, the page folds every written form down to a comparison key for the name itself: capital and small letters read the same, spaces and dashes slipped in or left out read the same, a decorated ⑦ or a raised ⁷ reads as 7, and lookalike letters from another alphabet (a Cyrillic а wearing Latin a’s clothes) read as the letter they imitate. Every form that folds into a claimed name gets the same refusal. That folding changes nothing you see — the claimed name itself stays displayed exactly as written.
  • It runs the other way, too. A name claimed in Arabic, Japanese, Spanish — any script at all — is protected in that form and in every form that folds into it. Nobody loses their name to a keyboard trick, and nobody steals one with one either.
  • A name is a claimed name, not a verified identity. The registry proves what name was claimed, when, and under what code’s fingerprint. It does not claim to prove who was holding the phone — the same honest label as everywhere else in this house.
Permanence — read this before you claimPermanent, owner-only, retired forever — and history never erases▾
  • A claim is permanent. Once a name is picked, it is picked — it stays in the registry as yours.
  • Only you can ever release your name — and only with your code. Nobody else can release, revoke, or reassign anyone’s claimed name. Not a host. Not a Dungeon Master. Not the people who run these pages. Ever.
  • One device holds ONE claimed name (the current ruling). Your device’s saved identity binds to a single claimed name — you cannot stockpile names or hold several identities on one device. This binds the claimed name only: running several characters under your one name in a game is unaffected and stays allowed.
  • Changing your name: you release the old name with your code and take a new name — one that is untaken and has never been claimed before. You can never take a name that is claimed now, or one that was ever claimed.
  • A released name is RETIRED, never re-issued. Because history attaches to it, it stays in the registry forever, marked formerly-claimed, so nobody else can ever wear a name with someone else’s record under it.
  • History does NOT erase with a name change. Renaming is a recorded event — in this registry and, mid-game, in the Tale. Every past entry keeps the name it was made under; nothing is rewritten. Your card shows the continuity in the open: “now <new name>, formerly <old name>.” A new name never launders an old record.
  • The registry is append-only. Claims, releases, renames, and handings are events in its history, and that history ships with the pages as part of the record. Nothing is ever deleted from it.
Your code — the one keyThe code that opens, releases, renames, and hands your name — the only secret in the system▾

At claim time you pick your own code: a phrase, a number, any code you can remember — your choice of form. That one code does both jobs: it opens your claimed name when you sit at a table, and it is required to release, rename, or hand the name. Only the code’s fingerprint (a SHA-256 hash) enters the registry; the code itself is never stored anywhere by the page except in your own device save, as part of your saved character, and in your own keeping.

Lose the code and the name stays yours forever — unreleasable by anyone. There is no back door and no override. That is the honest price of a lock nobody else can pick.

Entry #1 — ~~~>Tristan⁷⁷⁷ — is locked. It was first entered as Tristan⁷ and settled into this form in the open on Nov 15, 2026; both forms fold to this one claim and both are protected. Its owner’s code fingerprint is not baked into this version of the page yet, so until it is, the name simply cannot be sat under by anyone at all. That errs on the safe side: nobody can take it, full stop. When the owner’s fingerprint is baked in, the name opens for the owner on any device with their code — and stays shut for the world.

Claim your name on this deviceOne name per device, permanent — your code is the only key▾

Claim your name on this device

Checking this device…

Release or rename your claimed nameYour code is required. The old name retires forever; history does not erase.▾

Hand your name to someone elseNames can be handed — openly, with the key, on the record. It is the ONLY way a claimed name changes hands.▾

Handing is not releasing. A handed name never goes back into the wild. The handing is recorded in the registry in the open — handed from <owner> to <receiver>, with the date — and the record separates the eras: everything said under the name before the handing stays the giver’s era, everything after is the receiver’s, and the handing event printed between them means the two are never confused.

On handing, the receiver sets their OWN new code. The giver’s code retires — the giver no longer holds any key to that name.

Suffix or prefix: a handed name may be taken with a suffix or prefix — Jr., II, a house mark, a word before or after. That marked name is a new, linked claim: the registry shows its line — “of the line of <original name>, handed <date>” — the new wearer’s history is entirely their own under the marked name, and the marked name is a full claim with every protection on this page.

The dodge stays shut: an unrelated person adding a prefix or suffix to a claimed name to sneak around the claim still folds into the claimed name and is refused. A prefix or suffix makes a legitimate new name only through a recorded handing by the owner.

The Backlog — file your own public pastAn option, not a force. Only you can backlog yourself, only with your code, only as far as you choose.▾

Entirely optional. If you hold a claimed name on this device, you may attach pieces of your public past to your record — things you have publicly said or done — each labeled self-filed, with its source and its date. You choose the scope: how far back, which sources, all of it or some of it. Nobody can backlog anybody else, and an empty backlog costs a name nothing.

The example everybody knows — Ready Player OneA story, used purely as an example — the same law in a world built on claimed names▾

A story, used here purely as an example — the same law, in a world built on claimed names.

  • Parzival is Wade’s claimed name. Nobody else in the OASIS can be Parzival. In that world your name is your seat and your reputation — everything you are there stands under the one name you picked. That is this law, worn by a whole world.
  • Art3mis is a name with a number standing in for a letter — a 3 doing an E’s job, inside the name itself. Names written in any form of symbols are the same claim, which is why this page folds 3-for-E, a raised ⁷, lookalike letters from other alphabets, and every written form down into the one name they spell.
  • History rides on the name. Everything Parzival did stands under Parzival — and Sorrento can’t rename his way out of his record. A new name never launders an old one; the record stays under the name it was made with.
  • The handing: Halliday hands his world — and the mantle of Anorak — to the winner. Openly, by rules set in advance, with the line of succession on the record for everyone to see. Names and mantles pass by handing, never by grabbing.
  • IOI is the villain because it wants to own the layer underneath — everyone’s names, everyone’s records, the handle itself. This table’s law is the opposite: your name is yours, your record is yours, and nobody owns the layer under either.
Ultimate Accountability — why Entry #1 keeps its shapeThe copyable form kept on purpose, so every word under it can be held to account▾

The owner of ~~~>Tristan⁷⁷⁷ was shown plainer forms of the name — forms that sit quietly in an ordinary chat bubble — and kept this one, on purpose. The reasoning is the owner’s own: anything said under this name can be copied and pasted back, word for word — so keep it, and let it keep its owner accountable at all times.

Here is the mechanism, explained in the open. In a chat app, three tildes in a row (~~~) are a signal: everything after this is a code block. So a message that begins with this name does not arrive as a normal bubble — it arrives boxed, as a copyable card, with a copy button on it, one tap from anyone’s clipboard. The tildes are spent as the frame and never even show. The owner knows all of that — and keeps the form anyway, because of it: every word said under the name travels exactly as it was said, with nothing softened and nothing paraphrased, and the record can hold the speaker to every one of those words, at all times. The owner’s name for that choice is the title of this layer: Ultimate Accountability.

It is not a trick reserved for one name. The mechanism is printed here so anybody else can do the same with theirs: pick a name — anything you can type — claim it under the law on this page, and then say what you say under it knowing all of it can be pasted back verbatim. That is accountability you choose for yourself, explained in the open so anyone can choose it too.

And it fits the rest of this law. The words themselves were always copyable — a copy was never what a claim had to stop. What a copy cannot carry is the claim underneath: the code only the owner knows, and the record of what was actually done under the name. Words copy for free; the doing stays attached to the name that did it.

The full stack — the same for everybodyFive layers, one standard — visible string, watermark, exactness, conferred look, code▾

Every claimed name gets the whole stack, on equal terms — not just Entry #1, not just early seats. Five layers, one standard:

  1. A distinctive visible string — your name, anything you can type, stored and displayed exactly as typed.
  2. An optional watermark — invisible marks inside the string, declared in the open (see below).
  3. Exactness checking at the gate — the two jaws: a fold match is an imitation and is refused; only the byte-exact codepoint string is the true name.
  4. The conferred look — a registry mark and a styling the page confers on the proven seat only. You choose your own at claim time from the built-in kit: a mark (star, diamond, moon, tower, leaf) and a motion (rise, glow, wave, or steady).
  5. Your code — the one key that opens the name, and the only secret in the whole system.

The watermark doctrine, in its owner’s shape: a name can be hidden, and it can be known that it is hidden. The watermark is hidden in the name — and it is not a secret that it is there. It is a declared safety feature, like the watermark in paper money: there for safety, printed into the material, and checkable by anyone. The registry entry openly shows a “Watermarked” note when a name carries one; the owner chooses the payload at claim time; and the registry’s exact codepoint spelling — one tap on “Exact spelling” in the registry above — is the public record anyone can check a string against: match, folds-only, or no match. Its safety is provenance and detection, never secrecy: a hand-made fake lacks the watermark, and a copy carries it and confesses its source. One honest limit, printed at full size: a paste carries the watermark through these pages, which never strip invisible marks — but some outside apps do strip them, and a string that has passed through such an app may arrive with its watermark gone. The check above will then honestly read folds-only or exact-without-watermark, never a false match.

The conferred look — a copy stands nakedThe page confers the look on the proven seat only; the identical string elsewhere renders plain▾

The look is conferred by the page, never carried by the string. When a seat has proven its claim — the device holds the claim, the presented string is byte-exactly the recorded name, and the code’s fingerprint checks out — the page renders that player’s name with its standing: the registry mark beside it, in the style its owner chose, and the name’s own motion treatment. The identical string typed by anyone else renders plain — no mark, no motion. A text copy loses the life. A screenshot freezes one frame of it. An impostor at the table stands visibly unmarked next to the original. A copy stands naked.

Entry #1’s design is the launch treatment. When ~~~>Tristan⁷⁷⁷ is conferred, the three tildes ripple like streaming streaks, the > gives a slow forward pulse, “Tristan” stands solid, and the three superscript 7s climb one-two-three in a slow staggered loop, each lifting a step higher — and the whole treatment burns silver: bright, cool, white-silver flame, with a darker edge on light grounds so it stays readable, and a small silver registry mark beside it showing it is Entry #1. That design is conferred by the page for the proven seat only — and any claimant can design their own standing the same way, from the kit at claim time. Same stack, same kit, everybody.

The two jaws — no lookalike has anywhere to liveFold refuses imitations; exact decides what is the name — the Cyrillic а worked example is inside▾

The gate checks every name with two jaws, and a lookalike is caught by both:

  • Jaw 1 — FOLD. Any string that folds onto a claimed name is treated as an imitation of that claim and refused without the owner’s code. Folding reads through the disguises: Cyrillic and Greek lookalike letters, decorated and fullwidth digits, slipped-in separators and spaces, accents, and case all fold down to the same key. A folded imitation can never register as a “different” name — the fold map covers the confusable twins of every letter in Entry #1’s name, and the decorated-digit family for its 7s.
  • Jaw 2 — EXACT. Only the byte-exact codepoint string recorded in the registry is the true name, and the conferred look is applied only on an exact codepoint match and a passing code proof — never on a fold match.

The worked example: write the name with a Cyrillic а — Tristаn⁷, where the “а” is U+0430, not the Latin a (U+0061). To every eye it is identical. It is still not the name: different codepoints, no code behind it, no look on it. As a new name, Jaw 1 refuses it as an imitation. As a costume at the table, Jaw 2 leaves it plain and unmarked. There is nowhere for it to live.

The Backlog — an option, not a forceOpen as much of your public past as you choose — self-filed, labeled, never required▾

An option, not a force — open as much of your past as YOU choose. A claim owner may, entirely by their own choice, attach their public past to their record: things they have publicly said or done — public posts, public statements, the public record — filed under their claimed name, in the registry history and the Tale record, where anyone at the table can read what the owner themselves put there.

  • The owner chooses the scope. How far back, which sources, all of it or some of it — that is the owner’s call, item by item, and it can grow whenever they choose. Nobody else sets it.
  • Nobody can backlog anybody else. Filing is proven the same way as everything else here — your own code, or your proven seat. There is no form, anywhere on this page, for putting something on another person’s record.
  • Never required, never a condition. A backlog is not the price of a seat, a claim, a mark, or a look. A name with an empty backlog stands in full standing, exactly as claimed.
  • Every item is labeled self-filed, with its source and its date — what it is, where it stands in public, and when it was said or done, printed beside it. The label is part of the item and never comes off.
  • The record law applies: the backlog is append-only. An item, once filed, is not erased; if something filed turns out wrong, the correction is filed beside it, in the open, and both stand.
  • Public means public. The backlog is a door the owner opens onto their own already-public past. It reaches nothing private, and opening it a crack opens exactly that crack — no more.

Why would anyone choose it? For the same reason Entry #1 keeps its shape: a record you opened yourself, about yourself, in your own words, cannot be sprung on you. What is already on the record — filed by you, labeled by you — is simply the past, standing where you put it.

This device’s registry historyAppend-only — the claims made on this device, recorded here▾

Claims made on this device are recorded here, append-only, and ride with this device’s copy until they are baked into the published registry as the pages update. A claim protects you at a table from the moment the host’s page knows it — and inside any one table, the first claim of a name is final for that run, whether or not it is in the registry yet.

No claims have been made on this device yet.

The honest edge, printed at full size: a page with no server cannot stop someone who deliberately builds a tampered copy to host a rogue table. What this law kills is impersonation at every real table run from these pages — the host’s copy checks every name as people join — and the claimed-name label covers the rest.

Resuming restores the game on this device as it was — tale, characters, tokens, scene, pouch, rules. Other players’ characters come back as “not here” (locked, untouched) until those players sit down again. Your deliberate saves in Your Saves are never touched by autosave.

Characters at this table

A character belongs to the story, not to a device. One seat can run a whole party, and control of any character can be passed — tap a character to open their card and pass control. The page sets no cap on party size; if your table wants a limit, it lives in your House Rules. If a player steps away, their characters cease to be in the scene — tokens off the stage, cards locked — while their state is held exactly as left, untouched, until they return.

No characters yet — yours appears here when you sit down.

Party Items The Pouch

The party’s shared things, visible to everyone. Quest items live here, in the pouch — not on one character’s card — so the story can never be locked inside an offline character’s pockets. Any character who is in the game can use what the party holds. Personal gear stays on a character’s card and follows the away rule.
