Dungeon Master The Mantle

No Dungeon Master yet — the host takes the mantle when a table opens.

The Host holds the table open; the Dungeon Master runs the story. They start as the same person, but the mantle can pass to any seat — the two roles are never the same job.

House Rules

The rules serve the story. Play them as written, bend them, or rewrite them — if the whole table agrees, it’s legal here.

This page hands you dice, a story, and a table — it never enforces a rulebook. The rules live with the players.

Voting default, housed here: at Table votes, a simple majority of the people seated (and eligible to vote) carries a vote, and a carried kick needs the Dungeon Master or host to let the person back before they can rejoin that session. The Dungeon Master can bend both rules with the controls right here. This is only the default: any vote's caller can set that vote's own way of being decided — and its own timer, or open time — when they call it, and the vote is then read by its own setup.

Not housed here, on purpose: anonymity is chosen per vote, by its caller, when the vote is called — it is printed on that vote's face before anyone casts. And handed voting authority belongs to each giver alone: no house rule can grant it, move it, or take it back — only the giver can, from their own seat, at Table votes.

Only the Dungeon Master or host can change these — and any change goes into the Tale, on the record.

NPCs Run by the Dungeon Master

Every table has its folk. An NPC is a character like any other — card, token, and all — whose controller is the Dungeon Master (or, solo, the page’s story engine). Handing an NPC to a player is the same pass-control act as any character.

No NPCs yet.

The Tale

One story scroll, watched by the whole table as it grows. Gold entries are the Dungeon Master’s narration; dice land here for everyone.

Tap a die to roll it for the whole table. New to dice? “d20” means a 20-sided die — the main one for trying risky things (higher is better; 20 is a spectacular success, 1 is a fumble). Smaller dice (d4–d12) are usually for damage and healing. Full guide in Layer 5 of “Never played before?” above. Roll only when the outcome is uncertain — your DM will usually tell you which die.

Posts and dice rolls carry the acting character’s name. Switch any time — everybody can post, roll, move, and talk at once. This table never enforces turns.

Table Talk

Out-of-character chat — plans, jokes, and the fallback when voice is off.

💾 Save & go back

How saving works hereThree kinds of save, three separate places — none of them ever overwrites another quietly▾

Everything here lives on this device only — nothing is saved on any server. Three different things, kept in three separate places, and none of them ever overwrites another quietly:

  • Autosave — the game saves itself, below. It only ever writes to its own one slot.
  • Your Saves — games you deliberately save under a name. Each one is its own slot and stays exactly as saved until you delete it or deliberately save over that one save.
  • A save file — a portable copy you download, to carry a game to another night or another device.

While a table is open, the whole game — the tale, characters and where their tokens stand, the scene, the party pouch, house rules, and the clock — saves itself to this device every 30 seconds and shortly after anything important changes. The host’s device holds the shared table’s autosave; every player’s device also keeps its own copy of the tale and characters. Close the page by accident and your game is still here.

Autosave: nothing saved on this device yet.

Go back / redoStep the whole game back to how it was a moment ago — or forward again▾

Went too far? Go back steps the whole game — tale, hit points, tokens, scene, pouch, all of it — to how it was a moment ago, and Redo steps forward again. Going back never destroys the road forward until somebody plays something new. At a live table the host (or the Dungeon Master) runs go back / redo, so the whole table goes back together; solo, it’s yours.

No steps to go back to yet.
Your Saves — your shelfGames you deliberately save under a name, kept on this device▾

Save the current game under a name and keep it. Saves never save over each other by accident: saving with a name you’ve used before simply adds a new dated entry — the old one stays untouched. The only way a save is ever replaced is the deliberate one: pick that one save below, tap “Save over this one,” and confirm. Deleting likewise only ever removes the one save you pick and confirm.

No saves on your shelf yet — this device is holding none.

Portable save fileDownload the whole game as one file; load it back on any device▾

Download the whole current game as one file, keep it anywhere, and load it back here on any device to pick the game up. Loading a file (or a save from your shelf) replaces the game currently on this page — go back can’t undo a load, so autosave or save to Your Saves first if this game matters.

How the table works

Playing, in four stepsCreate, share the code, sit down, play▾
  1. One person creates a table. They become the Host and the first Dungeon Master, and get a 5-letter table code.
  2. Everyone else types the code on their own device and sits down. The code is the door — no accounts, no links to chase. (A copy of this page served from a plain address can also carry the code as ?table=CODE at the end of its address; the code itself is what matters.)
  3. Play. The Dungeon Master sets scenes and narrates; every player posts actions, rolls dice, drags their token, and talks by voice or text. Everything lands for the whole table at once.
  4. The game saves itself. Autosave keeps the whole game on each device as you play (see Save & go back), you can shelve named games in Your Saves, download a portable save file, and “Save the tale” still downloads the story alone as a readable text file.

The Table Clock is a real-life timer for the real people at the table — timed turns, a bridge that falls in sixty real seconds, or simply how long the session has run. The page provides the clock; the game decides what it means.

The story engine is the players themselves — there is no AI game master here, and that is the point of a round table. More games can come to the table later; this first table is for Dungeons & Dragons–style role-playing.

How the connection worksTwo plain sentences, no jargon left hanging▾

PeerJS is the free public relay that introduces the devices to each other — it hands out the table codes and makes the first knock on the door, and then steps aside.

WebRTC is the browser’s own device-to-device connection — once introduced, the story, dice, tokens, and voices travel straight between the players’ devices, not through a server.

The honest limitsRead these at full size — they are part of how this works▾
  • The table is held by the host’s open page — no host, no table. If the host closes their page, the table closes for everyone (guests keep the tale they witnessed and can save it).
  • Voice travels device-to-device, and a few strict networks may block direct connections. If voice won’t connect on a network, text always works.
  • Voice works best in a real browser window — an app’s built-in viewer may block the microphone.
  • Nothing is saved on a server. The tale exists on the players’ devices (each device keeps a copy of what it witnessed, on that device only), in the autosave and Your Saves on those same devices, and in the downloads you make.
  • Voice works best with up to about eight people at a table — every voice connects to every other voice, so very large tables can strain a phone. The seats themselves are never capped; the table is infinite.
  • Guests who drop get a few automatic tries to reconnect before the table gives up on their seat.
Bounce in, bounce out — and no enforced turnsCharacters stay where they were left; structure is the table’s choice▾
  • Step away and your character is simply not here. If you are not in the game, your character cannot be messed with — and in the world, it ceases to exist until you are back. Its token comes off the tabletop, it cannot be spoken to, harmed, helped, looted, or used as a roadblock, and the tale moves around where it stood as if it were not there. The Tale says it plainly: “<character> is not here.”
  • Its state is preserved exactly. Card, hit points, level, last token position — held by the host’s table state exactly as left. The card stays readable (looking is not messing) but locked: no edits. Nobody can touch an away character — not other players, not the Dungeon Master: no acting as them, no moving them, no hit-point changes, and no passing their control. Control can only be passed by a controller who is present, and the DM cannot reassign an absent player’s character.
  • Return and it exists again. Come back with the same table code and your saved card, and your characters are simply here again — tokens restored to the exact spots they were left in, state untouched. The Tale notes it: “<character> is here again.”
  • Honest boundary: a character’s held state lasts while the table is open. If the host closes the table, the session ends — and Save-the-tale is the record.
  • NPCs follow their controller. An NPC ceases only when its controller leaves. If the Dungeon Master leaves, the mantle falls back to the host, and the old DM’s NPCs pass to the new DM’s control — unless your House Rules say otherwise.
  • No enforced turns, ever. The default state of this table is open, simultaneous, freeform play — everybody can post, roll, move, and talk at once. If your table wants strict turns or initiative, run it yourselves and write it in the House Rules; the page will never impose it.
  • Control can be passed. A present controller can hand any character they run to another seat at any time, and the Dungeon Master can reassign any character whose controller is present. The hand-off is announced in the Tale. An away character’s control can never be passed — see the away rule above.
Saving, autosave, and going backWhere your game lives, and how the three kinds of save never collide▾
  • Autosave is the heartbeat. Every 30 seconds while a table is open — and shortly after anything important changes — the full game (tale, characters, token positions, scene, party pouch, house rules, clock) writes itself to this device only. The status line in Save & go back says when it last saved, in plain sight.
  • Resume. Reopen the page with an autosave present and you’re offered “Resume your last game.” It restores the game on this device; players who aren’t here come back under the away rule — present in the record, locked, untouched — and the clock comes back paused so no time is lost or invented.
  • Your Saves never clobber each other. Every named save is its own slot. Saving under a name you’ve used before adds a new dated entry and leaves the old one exactly as it was. A save is replaced only when you pick that specific save, tap “Save over this one,” and confirm — your own hand, on purpose, one save at a time. Autosave lives in its own separate slot and never touches Your Saves; Your Saves never touch the autosave.
  • Go back / redo. The page remembers recent states of the whole game. Go back steps everything back together; redo steps forward again — until new play branches off, at which point the old forward road is gone. At a live table the host or Dungeon Master runs it, so nobody’s screen disagrees.
  • Clearing. “Clear the tale copy & autosave” in Page settings wipes the witnessed tale and the autosave from this device. Your Saves are yours to delete one by one from the shelf — clearing never reaches into the shelf behind your back.
Claimed namesOne name, one owner, one code — the standing rule for everyone▾
  • Once a name is claimed on any table, it is claimed on all tables. A claim can be made right at any table with the claim form on this page; it is recorded in that table’s Tale record and in the registry’s append-only history with its date, and it travels to all tables as registry updates ship with new published versions — from then on every table enforces it. If the same name is claimed at two tables before an update ships, the first recorded claim wins and the later claim must choose another name; until an update lands, the room-level first claim protects the table where the claim was made.
  • Anyone can claim one name, and a name is unrestricted — any language, any script, emoji, symbols, spaces, punctuation, mixed scripts, long or short, anything you can type — and no one else can sit under it at any table run from these pages. The name is stored and displayed exactly as written, every decoration intact. Folding is only a comparison key for checking claims — case, spaces, dashes, decorated digits, and lookalike letters all read as the same key, so no spelling trick steals or loses a name — and it never alters, trims, or rejects a name for its shape. The gate refuses for exactly two reasons: the name folds onto somebody else’s live claim without their code, or it folds onto a retired name. Every other name, however wild, is welcome — the law protects names, it doesn’t police them.
  • A claim is permanent. Only the owner can release it, and only with their one self-chosen code — the same code that opens the name at a table. Not a host, not the DM, not the people who run the pages. Lose the code and the name stays yours forever, unreleasable by anyone.
  • One claimed name per device (the current ruling). Several characters under your one name are fine — several claimed names are not.
  • Released names retire forever and can never be worn again; a rename takes a new name that has never been claimed, is recorded in the open, and never erases history — cards read “now <new>, formerly <old>.”
  • Names can be handed — owner’s code, recorded in the open, receiver sets a new code — and a handed name may be worn with a suffix or prefix as a new, linked claim “of the line of” the original. An unrelated person adding a prefix or suffix to dodge a claim still folds into the claimed name and is refused.
  • Entry #1 is ~~~>Tristan⁷⁷⁷ — first entered as Tristan⁷, settled in the open on Nov 15, 2026, with both forms protected under the one claim — locked until its owner’s code fingerprint is baked in; until then nobody can sit under it at all. The full law, the registry, and the claim forms live in Claimed Names, right below Take your seat.
  • The Backlog is an option, not a force. A claim owner may — by their own choice alone, proven by their code — attach their public past (public posts, statements, the public record) to their record, each item labeled self-filed with its source and date, append-only under the same record law. The owner chooses the scope; nobody can backlog anybody else; it is never required and never a condition of a seat or a claim.
  • The full stack is the standard for every claimed name — visible string, optional declared watermark, exactness at the gate, the conferred look, and the owner’s code — available to every visitor on equal terms. The gate works in two jaws: anything that folds onto a claim is an imitation and is refused; the conferred look (registry mark + the styling its owner chose at claim time — Entry #1’s is the silver launch treatment) is applied only on a byte-exact codepoint match with a passing code proof, never on a fold match. Unproven seats render plain: a copy stands naked. The watermark is hidden in the name, and it is not a secret that it is there — the registry shows it and anyone can check a string against the exact codepoint spelling (match / folds-only / no match). The only secret in the system is the claim code.
Solo play and NPCsWhat the page’s story engine is — and is not▾

Solo, the page deals you a starting scene and a small cast of NPCs with cards and tokens. When you talk to or act toward an NPC, a die shades their reaction — warm, wary, or hostile — and their line is drawn from written banks inside this page that fit their nature. Light narration prompts keep the tale moving between your actions. It is a story engine, not a thinking mind — no server, no live AI, no fake promises. At a group table, NPCs are run by the Dungeon Master instead, who can speak in the Tale as any NPC they control.

What are we missing?

Tell us what this table needs: a game it should hold, a tool the Dungeon Master is reaching for, a rule that gets in the way, anything that’s wrong. Whole needed topics become new pages.

Just talk. Nobody has to phrase anything “appropriately” here — no grammar, no polish, no right way to say it. Say what you like and what you don’t like however it comes out: fragments, rambles, changing your mind mid-thought. All of it is considered on its substance; nothing is judged on how it was said. The door takes it from there.

How the microphone works, honestlyYour browser's own speech service, stays on while you scroll — and its one honest limit▾

How the microphone works, honestly: one tap starts it — your browser asks permission once — and it uses your browser’s own speech service to turn your voice into text. It stays on while you scroll and use the whole page: keep reading, keep playing, and say what you’re not seeing the moment you notice it; your words keep landing in the box above, and a listening bar follows you so you can stop it from anywhere. A second tap on the microphone button stops it. This page records nothing and sends nothing while you talk — your words become text in the box, and only what you choose to submit travels from this page, exactly as with typing. One honest limit, stated plainly: the transcription is done by your browser’s speech service, and most browsers — Chrome is the big one — send your voice audio to their maker’s servers to turn it into text; some other browsers and devices do it on the device itself. This page has no say in which yours does. If you’d rather your voice go nowhere at all, typing works exactly the same. Where a browser or an app’s built-in viewer cannot do live dictation, the line above the button says so plainly and typing works as always — a real browser window (Chrome or Safari itself) is the reliable door, the same note this page carries for voice at the table.

First, check what’s already there

That is this door’s one rule, and it runs exactly the same for talked words as for typed ones: before yours posts, look over the Poster Board. If your point is already standing there, add your voice to that thread instead of starting a twin. If it isn’t there, post yours.
